questions.explanation: The first law gives delta U = Q - W = 500 J - 200 J = 300 J, a rise, since the energy arriving as heat exceeds the energy leaving as work. The tempting wrong answer 700 J adds the work instead of subtracting it, and -300 J puts the sign on the heat rather than on the work. In joules the arithmetic is a plain subtraction, but the sign follows from whether each quantity crosses the boundary inward or outward, which is why the convention has to be fixed first.

questions.explanation: The heater delivers E = P t = (700 W)(60 s) = 42,000 J, and the water needs that energy to change temperature, so delta T = Q/(m c) = 42,000/((1.0 kg)(4200 J/(kg K))) = 42,000/4200 = 10 K. Adding the power and the time instead of multiplying gives (700 + 60) J = 760 J and then only 760/4200 = 0.18 K, and dividing the power by the mass gives 700 K, which has forgotten the time entirely. The 10 K step is also 10 degrees Celsius, since temperature differences carry the same number in both units.
questions.hint: Turn the power and the time into an energy, then use Q = m c delta T.

questions.explanation: For a closed system every joule that crosses the boundary counts: 1200 J arrives as heat, 500 J leaves as work and 700 J leaves as waste heat, so delta U = Q - W = 1200 J - (500 J + 700 J) = 0 J, and a machine in steady operation neither stores nor loses energy. The tempting wrong answer that keeps the 700 J forgets that the waste heat is a second exit rather than a store, and a machine that kept 700 J each second would heat up without bound. The 500 J answer counts only the work and pretends the hot exhaust carries nothing away.
